stem: A digital portal achieves zero errors on automated accessibility scans, yet users who rely on screen magnifiers find its complicated layout impossible to navigate. What does this demonstrate?

options.text: Automated scans check the requirements that matter most, and the rest are optional best practice.
options.rationale: Automated tools can check only a subset of WCAG requirements; the criteria they cannot test are still required, not optional.

options.text: Technical compliance with automated rules does not guarantee a usable experience.
options.shortLabel: Technical compliance does not guarantee usability
options.rationale: Automated tools check only a fraction of accessibility requirements and cannot evaluate human cognitive usability, task flow, or layout coherence.

options.text: Screen magnifier users are not covered by WCAG, so their experience falls outside the scope of compliance.
options.rationale: WCAG applies to all web content users, including people who enlarge text or use screen magnifiers; its text-resizing criterion speaks directly to them.

options.text: The scan result proves conformance, so the difficulty comes from the users' assistive technology.
options.rationale: A passing scan does not prove conformance; the barrier can sit in the layout and interaction design rather than in the user's software.

explanation: Accessibility compliance and usability are complementary but distinct concepts. A website can achieve a passing score on automated technical checklists while remaining confusing, clunky, or practically unusable for people with disabilities. Manual evaluation and functional testing with users are indispensable.

references.title: W3C WAI: Involving Users in Evaluating Web Accessibility
